about: The prayer calls the bread “hóstia” — Latin for a sacrificial victim, not for bread; already here, before the consecration, the gift is spoken of in the words of sacrifice. The priest lists whom he offers it for, and the order is telling: his own sins first, then “all here present” — circumstántes, literally those standing round — and last all the faithful, living and dead. The three words for his own fault are not synonyms either: peccáta are deeds done, offensiónes are affronts given to someone, negligéntiæ are neglects — the things left undone.

s01.narrative: The priest takes the paten with the host and raises it; at Solemn Mass the deacon hands it to him. The priest says the prayer silently.

s02.translation: Receive, holy Father, almighty eternal God, this spotless host, which I, thy unworthy servant, offer to thee, my living and true God, for my innumerable sins, offences and negligences, and for all here present, and also for all faithful Christians living and dead: that it may profit me and them unto salvation, into life everlasting. Amen.

w001.function: The imperative opens the prayer; its object, “hóstiam” (w009), stands eight words away.

w003.function: The prayer addresses the Father — not the Trinity, as “Súscipe, sancta Trínitas” will after the Lavábo.

w004.function: The vocative of a 3rd declension adjective is identical with the nominative; the address to the Father settles it.

w006.function: Two addresses in one: “sancte Pater” and “omnípotens ætérne Deus” — three adjectives and two nouns, all vocative.

w007.function: It points at what the priest is holding: not a sacrifice in general but this one.

w010.function: A relative in the accusative because it is the object of “óffero” (w015); it takes gender and number from “hóstiam” (w009).

w011.function: Latin drops the subject pronoun unless it is stressed — and here it is: it is I, unworthy, who offer.

w015.function: A compound of ob- and fero (to carry): to carry a thing before someone. This whole part of the Mass is named from it.

w019.function: The adjective, not the verb “I live” — agreement with “Deo” (w017) decides it.

w021.function: A biblical turn of phrase — the words are Paul's (1 Thess 1:9): the living and true God, as against idols.

w024.function: The form is dative as well as ablative; the preposition “pro” (w022), which governs the ablative, decides.

w026.function: The second of three nouns of fault: not the deed itself but the affront given to someone.

w028.function: The third kind of fault: not what was done wrongly but what was left undone.

w029.function: One “my” covers all three nouns; the form marks no gender and the nouns are of two, so no gender is claimed here.

w033.function: A participle used as a noun: literally “those standing round”. This is the Church Latin word for the congregation.

w035.function: “sed et” is not “but and” but the settled “and moreover”: the list widens beyond those present.

w039.function: Both adjectives stand as nouns here: the faithful Christian people.

w041.function: A stronger “and” than et — it binds the two into one pair: the living and the dead together.

w042.function: From defúngi — to discharge, to have done with; the dead are those who have finished with life.

w044.function: Dative of advantage with “profíciat” (w047): to whom it is to be of profit.

w046.function: The form is dative as well as ablative and marks no gender; the masculine dative rests on the sense — those just named.

w047.function: Its subject is the host: may it be of profit. Subjunctive after “ut” (w043).
